justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'd assume was the prevailing level around 3,100–3,120 at the time of the forecast. For the 1-day horizon, the estimate of 3,118 essentially anchors near the most recent observed price, reflecting the strong mean-reversion tendency of equity indices over very short horizons and the absence of any scheduled catalysts that would justify a large directional move. The 1-week estimate of 3,130 incorporates a slight positive drift consistent with the long-run historical equity risk premium, while the 1-month estimate of 3,155 extends that drift further. In all three cases, the upward bias is modest because equity indices tend to grind higher over time in expectation, but the magnitude of any single move is highly uncertain.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the well-established square-root-of-time scaling of volatility. At the 1-day level, a roughly ±65-point interval (90% CI) corresponds to an implied daily move of about 2%, which is consistent with typical S&P 500 realized volatility in the 15–20% annualized range. By one month, the interval opens to roughly ±285 points, or about 9% on either side, which is similarly consistent with that volatility assumption scaled over approximately 21 trading days. The uncertainty also reflects ambiguity about the macroeconomic backdrop, including Fed policy expectations, earnings trends, and global growth signals, any of which can shift meaningfully over a multi-week period.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes well outside the stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected escalation in geopolitical conflict, a sudden credit event or financial contagion (such as a major bank failure or sovereign debt stress), or a surprisingly hawkish Fed pivot could easily produce a drawdown exceeding 10%, pushing the index below 2,800. A sharp deterioration in economic data suggesting recession could have a similar effect. On the upside, a definitive resolution to trade tensions, a dovish Fed surprise, or stronger-than-expected earnings could produce a rally that breaks above 3,440. These tail risks are precisely why I'd caution that the stated 90% confidence intervals, while constructed carefully, still leave 10% probability mass in the tails where outcomes can be quite extreme.
